intro: Sleeping Beauty’s pavane opens Ma mère l’Oye with twenty quiet bars for four hands at one piano. The melody passes between the two players as simply as a story told at bedtime.

sections.label: A · A low tune, a high answer
sections.mNote: The lower player begins; the upper player answers

sections.label: B · The upper melody keeps walking
sections.mNote: Quavers carry the tune through the middle of the keyboard

sections.label: A′ · The high tune returns
sections.mNote: The opening answer returns over gently repeated notes

cues.title: Two people, one piano
cues.text: The lower player begins alone with a small, stepwise tune. The upper player answers, then reaches higher for a melody over softly repeated notes. Both parts fit comfortably under the hands.
cues.evidence: Durand piano-duet score (1910), pp. 2–3, bars 1–8: Seconda opening, Prima answer and high melody from bar 5. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/17620
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Children at the piano
cues.text: Ravel dedicates the suite to Mimie and Jean Godebski. At the first public performance, on 20 April 1910 in Paris’s Salle Gaveau, Jeanne Leleu and Geneviève Durony sit at the piano. They are eleven and fourteen.
cues.evidence: IRCAM work catalogue: dedication, date, venue, performers and ages. https://brahms.ircam.fr/fr/work/ma-mere-l%27oye

cues.title: The high tune returns
cues.text: The earlier high melody returns over the same softly repeated accompaniment. Ravel lets it slow at the end, with a fermata over the last notes. The two players finish together.
cues.evidence: Durand piano-duet score, pp. 2–3, bars 17–20: return of bars 5–8, altered ending, Rall. and fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The tune walks down the keyboard
transitions.from: A · A low tune, a high answer
transitions.to: B · The upper melody keeps walking
transitions.how: The high answer descends into the middle of the keyboard. The upper player’s repeated accompanying notes stop, leaving a line of quavers above the lower player’s slower notes. Ravel keeps the quiet dynamic and the unhurried four-beat bar.

transitions.title: The high answer comes back
transitions.from: B · The upper melody keeps walking
transitions.how: The upper part returns to its high melody at pp, with gently repeated notes below it. The lower player restores the earlier accompaniment. A rallentando and a fermata lengthen the final bar.

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery. His mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He kept returning to the Basque coast, and Spain kept returning in his music: the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera that rocks through the Rapsodie espagnole, the clocks ticking in a Toledo shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. Two teachers then understood him: André Gedalge, who gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and Fauré, whose composition class he entered in January 1898. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, became the pianist his music needed. Viñes gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces their composer could never have played with comparable command.
